title: Your rhythm
hook: Five prayers can feel like five interruptions, or like the frame your day hangs on. Let's build the frame.

screens.text: A month in, the question changes from "How do I pray?" to "How do I keep this up?" The answer isn't more willpower. It's a rhythm.

**The five prayers are your frame.** Everything else (lessons, Qur'an, extra worship) fits around them, a little at a time. The deeds Allah loves most are the regular ones, even if they're small [Bukhari 6464].
bubbles: Allah doesn't burden anyone beyond what they can carry [Q 2:286].
So build a routine you could keep on your worst week, not your best.

screens.prompt: Drag the sun through a day
screens.text: Five windows, spread across your day. Each one is a spot to hang a habit on.

screens.prompt: Anchor each prayer to something you already do. Match each prayer to an example anchor.

pairs.right: Right after class or a shift block
Before you wind down for bed

screens.situation: Ana feels behind. Her new plan: all five prayers, every extra prayer she's heard of, an hour of Qur'an, and a 5 a.m. study session. Starting tomorrow.

options.text: Keep the five as the core, add one small extra (like 5 minutes of Qur'an), and grow slowly
options.feedback: Yes. A plan she can keep beats a perfect plan she drops in a week.

options.text: Go for the full plan while she's motivated
options.feedback: Kind instinct, but that's the classic path to burnout. Steady and small lasts.

options.text: Drop to fewer prayers until life calms down
options.feedback: Not quite. All five are due. The fix is fewer extras, not fewer prayers.

screens.title: Build your day around five prayers
steps: Open today's prayer times (set up on Day 2)
For each prayer, pick an anchor: something you already do around that time
Pick a spot for each one: home, work, school, the masjid
Set a discreet reminder for each prayer. Anchors beat alarms alone; use both at first
Choose ONE small extra for this week (5 minutes of Qur'an, or the after-prayer phrases coming up)
Plan Fajr: alarm across the room, and a bedtime that makes it possible
screens.done_text: That's your rhythm. Try it for a week, then adjust what doesn't fit.

screens.text: **After the salam, don't rush off.** Stay seated a moment. The Prophet ﷺ, when he finished a prayer, would ask Allah's forgiveness three times and then say a short line praising Him as the source of peace [Muslim 591].
bubbles: It's a humble way to close: you've just prayed, and you still turn to Allah for forgiveness. It takes about 15 seconds.

screens.when: Three times, right after the salam that ends each prayer [Muslim 591]. Then today's prayer phrase.

moves.text: Give the salam to the right…
…and to the left. Your prayer is done. Don't rush off.
Then today's prayer phrase, praising Allah as the source of peace.

screens.text: Five prayers as the frame, anchored to your day; one small extra at a time.
A rhythm you keep is worth more than a plan you admire. Slow and steady.

prayerPhrase.translit: Allahumma antas-salam wa minkas-salam, tabarakta dhal-jalali wal-ikram
prayerPhrase.meaning: O Allah, You are Peace, and peace comes from You. How blessed You are, Lord of majesty and honor.
prayerPhrase.when: After the salam, right after Astaghfirullah ×3 [Muslim 591]. Many people say "tabarakta ya dhal-jalali wal-ikram" (with "ya", O); that wording is narrated too [Muslim 592].

check.prompt: You're overwhelmed and want to cut back. What should go first?

options.text: The extras, not the five prayers
options.feedback: Right. All five are due. Trim the extras and keep them small and regular.

options.text: A couple of the daily prayers
options.feedback: Not quite. The five are the core. Fewer extras, not fewer prayers.

check.prompt: What did the Prophet ﷺ say right after finishing a prayer?

options.text: Astaghfirullah three times, then Allahumma antas-salam…
options.feedback: Right [Muslim 591]. About 15 seconds, after every prayer.

options.text: Nothing; he stood up straight away
options.feedback: Not quite. He asked forgiveness three times and praised Allah as the source of peace.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- The five prayers are the fixed core; extras are added slowly. Regular small deeds are most beloved to Allah [Bukhari 6464]; no soul is burdened beyond its capacity [Q 2:286]; each prayer has its time [Q 4:103].
- Over-zeal leads to burnout; converts do best adding one thing at a time [Field Guide ch. 9].
- After the prayer: *Astaghfirullah* ×3, then *Allahumma antas-salam wa minkas-salam, tabarakta dhal-jalali wal-ikram* [Muslim 591; Muslim 592 has "ya dhal-jalali"]. The Hanafi manual adds Ayat al-Kursi and *Subhan Allah*, *al-hamdu lillah*, *Allahu akbar* ×33 [First Instructions on Worship, appendix]; offer these only if the convert asks for more.
- Never present fewer than five prayers as acceptable (Q4 wording: "All five are due; pray each one with what you know so far").

**Likely questions**
- *"Plan around my schedule."* Ask for their typical day and today's prayer times; map each prayer to a gap and a spot. Keep it realistic.
- *"How do I wake up for Fajr?"* Earlier bedtime, alarm across the room, wudu by the bed, a friend's wake-up text. If they miss it, pray it as soon as they wake (Day 21).
- *"I keep missing Asr."* Find the anchor; pray early in the window; plan with work (Day 24).
- *"More remembrance after prayer?"* Offer the 33/33/33 tasbih as an optional extra, one at a time.

**Escalate:** schedules that seem to make a prayer impossible (night shifts, long surgeries, exams): general tips, then the imam.

**Don't**
- Don't stack a long list of extras.
- Don't suggest combining prayers to save time (not Hanafi practice; escalate).
